How Wi-Fi Fills a House: Wave Physics vs. the Planning Model

A 2.4 GHz router in a three-room house, computed two ways: by solving Maxwell's equations for the radio wave itself, and with the standard engineering model that Wi-Fi planners use. Both take their wall properties from the same international standard (ITU-R P.2040). Press Switch on to watch the wave leave the router at the speed of light and fill the house in its first 48 nanoseconds, switch between the models, move the router, and hover anywhere to read the signal.

Wave physics: a 2D finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) solution of Maxwell's equations for a continuous 2.4 GHz wave with a vertical electric field, on a 5 mm grid (5.5 million cells), run until it settled (the last two 20 ns windows differ by under 0.001 dB rms); shown in 2.5 cm pixels. Before use the solver was checked against the standard: on the same 5 mm grid, a plane wave through each wall build-up loses within 0.5 dB of the ITU-R P.2040 value (concrete 11.85 vs 11.40 dB, brick 5.97 vs 5.71, the others within 0.05), and in open air the field falls with distance exactly as theory predicts. Because it is 2D, the computed field spreads over circles instead of spheres; 10·log10(distance) is subtracted to give 3D spreading, which is exact for the direct wave and approximate for echoes. It has no floor, ceiling or furniture. Switch-on timeline: the same solver from the moment the router starts transmitting (its output rises over the first 1 ns), saved every 0.75 ns for the first 48 ns as the local strength averaged over each interval, in 5 cm blocks and 1 dB steps; black means below −95 dBm (the wave has not arrived yet). By 48 ns it matches the settled field to within about 1 dB (median difference under 0.1 dB). The timeline runs in slow motion: about 6 ns of real time per second. Planning model: free-space loss (Friis) plus, for every wall the straight line crosses, that wall's loss at normal incidence, as allowed by ITU-R P.1238 for site-specific models. The dashed line in the chart is P.1238's own residential distance model (N = 28, the 1.8–2 GHz row, the nearest to 2.4 GHz in the 2003 edition), with walls averaged in. Materials: ITU-R P.2040-4 (09/2025), Table 3, ε′ = a·f^b, σ = c·f^d at 2.4 GHz; wall loss from its slab (ABCD) method, eqs. 60–63. Power: 20 dBm EIRP, the European limit for 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi (ETSI EN 300 328 V2.2.2, clause 4.3.2.2.3), so −20.05 dBm at 1 m (free-space loss 40.05 dB). −67 dBm is the cell-edge level Cisco and Apple recommend for voice and video (Cisco white paper). The house is an example plan (10 × 7.5 m), not a measured home. · Highcharts.com
